posts.title: A small AI support inbox loop
posts.promise: Triage one kind of ticket, draft a sourced reply, and leave approval to a person.
posts.whatItIs: Auxx describes a support CRM where an agent can read tickets, retrieve relevant customer records and knowledge, draft replies, and update records. A beginner version could handle one narrow ticket type using a small sample inbox and a written procedure, rather than rebuilding the full CRM.
posts.whoPays: Hypothesis: a small online shop or support team with repetitive questions might pay for less routine inbox work. The supplied page does not establish paying customers or demand.
loop: A new test ticket or scheduled run starts the workflow.
The system finds the relevant customer record and approved policy text.
A written procedure routes the ticket to one supported category.
The model drafts a reply using retrieved material and marks uncertain cases.
A person reviews the draft and decides whether to send it.
The workflow records the category and outcome for later review.

posts.title: A human checked support inbox loop
posts.promise: Sort incoming questions and prepare reply drafts for a person to review.
posts.whatItIs: n8n is a workflow builder that connects services and can include AI steps. A small student version could take incoming support messages, label them by topic, and prepare a draft reply for review. A workflow is a set of connected steps that runs when an event occurs.
posts.whoPays: Hypothesis: a small online shop with a recurring support inbox might pay for setup or maintenance; the supplied page does not establish demand for this student service.
loop: A new test support email triggers the workflow.
Rules remove obvious junk and pass the message to a classifier.
The classifier assigns a topic and priority.
The workflow retrieves an approved answer note and drafts a reply.
A person reviews and sends the draft, correcting uncertain cases.
The workflow records the outcome for later review.

posts.title: Track GPU prices and specs in one view
posts.promise: Collect a small set of public GPU prices and compare them with published specifications.
posts.whatItIs: Flopper is a GPU hardware explorer. Its maker says it combines GPU specifications, workload estimates, and prices from dozens of providers. The maker also notes that reliable quotes for some large systems are difficult to obtain, so listings are not complete procurement quotes. A student version could track a few consumer GPUs and public provider pages, showing dated prices beside basic specifications. Small AI teams or hardware shoppers might pay for such a comparison, but this customer and willingness to pay are hypotheses. The automated part is checking selected pages and recording changes. A person should confirm the exact model, configuration, availability, and final price before relyin
posts.whoPays: Hypothesis: small AI teams or individuals comparing hardware may pay for a focused price and specification tracker; the source establishes no customers or revenue.
loop: Keep a manually reviewed list of GPU models and public provider pages.
Fetch the selected pages on a schedule and extract visible price and configuration text.
Store each observation with its URL and timestamp.
Compare new observations with prior ones and flag changes or missing prices.
Show a comparison with the published hardware specifications.
Have a person verify configuration, availability, and quote details before purchase.

posts.title: Catch failures in production AI agents
posts.promise: Turn agent traces into grouped findings and a human-reviewed root-cause report.
posts.whatItIs: Tessary is an open-source tool for teams running AI agents in production. Its repository describes receiving traces (records of an agent’s operations), checking them with classifiers, grouping related findings into cases, and investigating likely causes using trace evidence and, when connected, repository code. A small student project could accept test traces, apply a few simple checks, group matching alerts, and prepare a report for a developer. Teams operating AI agents are a plausible customer, but the sources do not establish who pays. The repeating work is trace checking and case preparation; a person still needs to confirm whether a finding is a real problem and choose any fix.
posts.whoPays: Hypothesis: teams operating production AI agents may pay for help finding and investigating failures; the repository does not establish paying customers or revenue.
loop: Receive an agent trace through an instrumentation endpoint.
Normalize the trace into a consistent format.
Run enabled classifiers and open findings when checks trigger.
Group related findings into a case.
Investigate the case using trace evidence and connected repository code when available.
Send the findings and explanation to a human owner, who decides whether and how to fix the system.

posts.title: Test AI phone agents with repeatable calls
posts.promise: Run a scripted call against a phone agent and receive a reviewable pass or fail result.
posts.whatItIs: VoiceGremlin is described by its maker as an API for testing AI systems that answer phone calls. A user supplies a phone number and a test case, such as checking whether the agent performs a requested behavior. The service calls the agent, has the two bots converse, and uses an LLM judge—a language model asked to assess the result—to return pass or fail for a software pipeline. A small student version could run one scripted scenario against a test phone agent and save the call outcome. Teams building voice agents are a plausible customer, but the source does not establish who pays or whether customers use it. The repeated loop can run without a person placing each test call, while a human st
posts.whoPays: Hypothesis: companies building AI phone agents may pay to check that their agents keep meeting defined behaviors; the source provides no customer or revenue evidence.
loop: An operator defines a test case and supplies a test phone number.
The API places a call to the phone agent being checked.
The test bot speaks with the phone agent about the scenario.
An LLM judge compares the conversation with the requested behavior.
The system returns a pass or fail result to a software pipeline.
A developer reviews unclear failures and updates the test or phone agent.

posts.title: Check whether docs work for AI agents
posts.promise: Scan a documentation URL for common access and format problems, then review a scorecard.
posts.whatItIs: Velu's agent-friendly documentation checker is described as scoring a documentation URL against the open Agent-Friendly Documentation Spec, using the spec's reference implementation called afdocs. The Show HN post names issues the spec is concerned with: pages rendered only in the browser, missing llms.txt or Markdown versions, soft 404 pages, and pages too large for an agent's context window. A beginner could build a small scheduled checker for one documentation site that records the score and lists detectable problems. Documentation teams are a plausible customer, but the source does not establish who pays. This is an audit and reporting loop, not an automatic documentation repair service.
posts.whoPays: Hypothesis: teams maintaining developer documentation may pay for recurring checks; the source does not establish customers or revenue.
loop: Read a configured documentation site URL.
Check pages for supported agent access and format signals.
Run the reference checker and save its score.
Compare the result with the previous scan.
Send a report when the score or detected issues change.
A documentation owner verifies findings and chooses any fix.

posts.title: Route visual feedback to a coding agent
posts.promise: Turn a marked-up staging page into an agent task with a reviewable status trail.
posts.whatItIs: CircleIt is described as a Chrome extension plus a Claude Code or Codex plugin. A teammate can mark an area on a page, explain the requested change, and send the screenshot, comment, and page metadata to a running coding agent. The source says the system matches the page address to a repository and reports status back in the sender's browser. A small student version could capture one staging page and open a proposed task for a developer's agent. Small product teams are a plausible customer, but that is a hypothesis. The loop handles intake and handoff; a human still needs to judge whether the requested change is correct and review code before release.
posts.whoPays: Hypothesis: small software teams that collect frequent website feedback may pay; no customer or payment evidence is given.
loop: A teammate opens a staging page and marks a visible issue.
Capture the screenshot, comment, page address, and relevant metadata.
Match the page address to a configured repository.
Send the feedback to the team's running coding agent after any required approval.
Show the sender the agent's status and response.
A developer reviews code changes and decides whether to merge.
